title: Red or Swollen Leg Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing an acutely red or swollen leg, distinguishing infection from vascular, venous, lymphatic, joint and traumatic causes, and supporting safe investigation, referral and follow-up.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, JRCALC, local DVT pathways, antimicrobial guidance or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: A rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection, including necrotising infection.
Acute limb ischaemia, threatened limb perfusion or compartment syndrome.
Deep vein thrombosis and symptoms suggesting pulmonary embolism.
Septic arthritis, deep abscess, osteomyelitis or another deep infection.
A limb-threatening diabetic foot problem.
Cellulitis or erysipelas and any portal of entry.
Venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, lymphoedema or another non-infectious mimic.
Trauma, haematoma, superficial thrombophlebitis, gout or inflammatory arthritis.
Loss of mobility, inability to self-care or inadequate support that changes disposition.
items.importantLimitation: Redness, warmth, swelling, fever, CRP and white-cell count are individually non-specific. No single finding reliably distinguishes cellulitis from DVT or another mimic.

sections.title: History prompts
sections.intro: Define the pattern, time course and likely anatomical source before labelling the presentation as cellulitis.

items.title: Distribution and time course
mustConfirmOrExclude: Exact onset and whether symptoms developed suddenly, gradually or on a background of chronic swelling or skin change.
Unilateral or bilateral involvement.
Exact starting point and whether redness or swelling is spreading.
Localised, linear, joint-centred, gaiter-region, foot-predominant or whole-leg involvement.
Whether swelling preceded redness or redness preceded swelling.
Previous similar episodes, previous diagnosis and response to antibiotics, elevation, compression or topical treatment.
Any marked change from the patient's usual leg appearance, size, mobility or function.

items.title: Symptoms and functional effect
mustConfirmOrExclude: Pain, itch, burning, heaviness or tightness, including which symptom predominates.
Local warmth, tenderness, throbbing or pain with movement.
Fever, rigors, malaise, confusion, reduced intake or other systemic deterioration.
Pain at rest, pain on weight-bearing and ability to stand, transfer and walk.
Pain centred on a joint and restriction of active or passive movement.
Severe or rapidly escalating pain, particularly when disproportionate to visible skin changes.
Chest pain, new breathlessness, haemoptysis, syncope or collapse.

items.title: Skin breach, exposure and trigger
mustConfirmOrExclude: Wound, ulcer, fissure, blister, pressure injury, puncture, injection, cannula site or recent procedure.
Interdigital cracking, maceration or fungal infection.
Bite, sting, new topical product, adhesive, dressing or compression garment.
Trauma, fall, direct blow, vigorous exercise or possible foreign body.
Exposure to fresh water, sea water, animal saliva or soil.
Recent travel or infection acquired outside the UK.
Purulent discharge, fluctuance or a previously drained abscess.

items.title: DVT and venous thromboembolism risk
mustConfirmOrExclude: Previous DVT or pulmonary embolism.
Active cancer or recent cancer treatment.
Recent major surgery, hospital admission or bed rest for at least 3 days.
Paralysis, paresis, plaster cast, lower-limb immobilisation or substantial reduction in mobility.
Pregnancy, postpartum state, combined hormonal contraception or hormone replacement therapy.
Long-distance travel or prolonged seated immobility.
Known thrombophilia or strong family history of venous thromboembolism.
Current anticoagulation, adherence, recent interruption and any bleeding risk.

items.title: Arterial and perfusion history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Sudden severe limb pain or abrupt deterioration.
New coldness, pallor, mottling, numbness or weakness.
Previous peripheral arterial disease, vascular surgery, angioplasty or amputation.
Intermittent claudication or rest pain.
Diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation and other vascular risk factors.
Recent tight bandage, cast or compression garment.

items.title: Background conditions and medicines
mustConfirmOrExclude: Chronic venous insufficiency, varicose veins, venous ulceration or previous venous intervention.
Lymphoedema, lymph-node surgery, radiotherapy or recurrent cellulitis.
Diabetes, neuropathy, previous diabetic foot disease or poor glycaemic control.
Heart failure, renal disease, liver disease or chronic bilateral oedema.
Inflammatory arthritis, gout, immunosuppression or recurrent skin disease.
Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants and recent antibiotics.
Calcium-channel blockers or other medicines that may contribute to oedema.
Known drug allergies, renal impairment and recent renal function when antimicrobial treatment may be required.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive or evolving features should change disposition and trigger JRCALC or the relevant urgent local pathway. This section identifies escalation triggers rather than reproducing emergency treatment.

items.title: Necrotising or rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection
urgentFeatures: Severe pain that is disproportionate to the visible skin findings.
Rapid progression over minutes or hours.
Skin necrosis, dusky discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae or anaesthesia.
Crepitus, marked oedema beyond the erythematous margin or systemic toxicity.
Significant deterioration despite appropriate initial treatment.
implications: Possible necrotising infection or deep soft-tissue infection; urgent hospital assessment is required.
items.importantLimitation: Early necrotising infection may have limited visible skin change. Do not rely on the absence of crepitus, fever or laboratory abnormalities.

items.title: Acute limb ischaemia or threatened perfusion
urgentFeatures: Sudden severe limb pain.
Cold, pale, cyanosed or mottled limb.
Absent or newly reduced pulses.
New paraesthesia, sensory loss or weakness.
Delayed capillary refill or rapidly deteriorating distal perfusion.
implications: Possible acute limb ischaemia; follow JRCALC and the emergency vascular pathway.
items.importantLimitation: Palpable pulses do not exclude more distal arterial disease, and chronic pulse deficits may complicate comparison. Interpret against the contralateral limb and baseline.

items.title: Compartment syndrome
urgentFeatures: Severe escalating pain after trauma, crush injury, reperfusion or tight immobilisation.
Pain on passive stretch.
Tense swollen compartment.
New sensory or motor deficit.
implications: Possible compartment syndrome; immediate hospital assessment is required.
items.importantLimitation: A pulse may remain present until late. Do not use preserved pulses to exclude compartment syndrome.

items.title: Septic arthritis, osteomyelitis or deep infection
urgentFeatures: Acutely hot, swollen and severely painful joint with marked restriction of active and passive movement.
Deep focal tenderness, fluctuance or suspected abscess.
Exposed bone, deep ulcer or a wound that probes towards bone.
Systemic illness, immunosuppression or recent joint procedure.
Persistent or recurrent inflammation despite appropriate treatment.
implications: Possible septic arthritis, osteomyelitis or deep abscess; urgent same-day specialist assessment is required.

items.title: Deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
urgentFeatures: A clinically suspected DVT requiring the local two-level Wells, D-dimer and ultrasound pathway.
New chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, syncope or collapse alongside possible DVT.
Marked whole-leg swelling, deep venous tenderness or substantial asymmetry with relevant risk factors.
implications: Follow the local DVT pathway. Where pulmonary embolism is suspected, follow JRCALC and the relevant emergency pathway.
items.importantLimitation: Cellulitis and DVT can coexist. An apparent skin infection does not remove the need for a DVT assessment when clinical suspicion remains.

items.title: Limb-threatening diabetic foot problem
urgentFeatures: Diabetic foot ulceration with fever, systemic deterioration or suspected sepsis.
Ulceration with limb ischaemia.
Gangrene.
Concern for deep soft-tissue or bone infection.
Rapidly progressive infection, extensive tissue loss or new neurovascular compromise.
implications: Use the diabetic-foot pathway. Limb-threatening or life-threatening disease requires immediate acute-service referral and notification of the multidisciplinary foot service according to local arrangements.

items.title: Systemic or functional deterioration
urgentFeatures: Physiological instability or rapidly worsening observations.
New delirium, reduced consciousness or marked functional decline.
Unable to stand, transfer or mobilise safely.
Unable to take or retain oral medication or fluids.
Inadequate support, safeguarding concern or inability to access required treatment and review.
implications: Disposition must account for physiological status, function, treatment access and support, even when the local leg findings initially appear uncomplicated.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Expose and compare both legs from the feet to above the knees. Interpret the findings alongside the history, observations, risk factors, progression and baseline appearance.

items.title: General assessment and mobility
howToTest: Assess overall appearance, distress, hydration and systemic illness.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation where clinically indicated.
Assess cognition and compare with baseline in older or frail patients.
Observe sitting, standing, transfers and walking where safe.
Assess ability to obtain, take and monitor treatment at home.
normal: Physiologically stable and not systemically unwell.
Alert and functioning at usual baseline.
Able to transfer and mobilise safely with usual support.
Able to take oral medication and engage with follow-up.
abnormal: Fever, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea or systemic deterioration.
New confusion, reduced intake or marked functional decline.
Unable to weight-bear, transfer or mobilise safely.
Unable to take treatment or no safe follow-up arrangement.
implications: Systemic or functional deterioration may indicate more extensive infection or another acute illness.
Unsafe mobility or inadequate support changes disposition even where no limb-threatening diagnosis is confirmed.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Systemic illness.
Functional deterioration.
Unsafe mobility.
Barriers to safe treatment and follow-up.

items.title: Inspection and distribution
howToTest: Expose both legs fully and compare colour, size, contour and chronic skin changes.
Identify the exact anatomical distribution and whether the process is unilateral or bilateral.
Determine whether the redness is diffuse, sharply demarcated, linear along a vein, centred on a joint, confined to the gaiter region or associated with a wound.
Inspect for scaling, crusting, weeping, excoriation, pigmentation, induration, varicosities, bullae, bruising, necrosis and lymphangitic streaking.
Inspect the plantar surface, heels and interdigital spaces.
Consider marking the erythematous margin with a single-use marker when cellulitis is treated and serial comparison is planned.
normal: No acute asymmetry, expanding erythema, skin breakdown or concerning chronic skin change.
No blistering, necrosis or lymphangitic spread.
abnormal: Expanding unilateral erythema and swelling.
Bilateral gaiter-region erythema with scaling, pigmentation or chronic oedema.
Linear erythema and tenderness following a superficial vein.
Bullae, dusky skin, necrosis or rapidly progressive discolouration.
Ulcer, wound, fissure, purulence or interdigital skin breakdown.
implications: Diffuse warmth and tenderness with an entry point may support cellulitis.
Bilateral chronic scaling and pigmentation favour venous disease or dermatitis over bilateral cellulitis.
Linear inflammation suggests superficial thrombophlebitis.
Bullae, necrosis or rapid progression raises concern for severe or deep infection.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Cellulitis or erysipelas.
Venous eczema or lipodermatosclerosis.
Superficial thrombophlebitis.
Necrotising or deep infection.
Portal of entry.
items.importantLimitation: Erythema may be less visible on darker skin tones. Give greater weight to warmth, swelling, tenderness, texture and change from the patient's baseline.

items.title: Palpation, temperature and tenderness
howToTest: Compare temperature using the backs of the hands at matching sites on both legs.
Palpate gently to identify whether tenderness is cutaneous, subcutaneous, venous, muscular, bony or joint-centred.
Assess for induration, fluctuance, crepitus and a tense compartment.
Determine whether pain is proportionate to the visible findings.
Palpate along the deep venous distribution only as part of an overall DVT assessment; do not repeatedly squeeze the calf.
normal: No significant temperature difference.
No focal deep tenderness, fluctuance, crepitus or disproportionate pain.
Soft compartments.
abnormal: Localised warmth and cutaneous tenderness.
Deep venous distribution tenderness.
Fluctuance suggesting a collection.
Crepitus, severe disproportionate pain or a tense compartment.
Focal bony or deep tissue tenderness.
implications: Warmth and superficial tenderness may support cellulitis but remain non-specific.
Deep venous tenderness contributes to the DVT Wells score when DVT is suspected.
Fluctuance may indicate an abscess requiring drainage.
Disproportionate pain, crepitus or tense swelling requires urgent escalation.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Deep vein thrombosis.
Abscess.
Necrotising infection.
Compartment syndrome.
Deep tissue or bone infection.

items.title: Swelling, oedema and limb measurement
howToTest: Determine whether swelling is localised, calf-predominant, whole-leg, foot-predominant or bilateral.
Assess for pitting by applying firm pressure over a bony area for several seconds and observing for a persistent indentation.
Assess whether oedema is confined to the symptomatic leg.
When DVT is suspected, measure calf circumference at the same defined level on both legs, 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity.
Document the exact measurement site and difference rather than recording only that one calf is larger.
normal: No clinically significant asymmetry.
No new unilateral pitting oedema.
Calf difference below 3 cm when measured correctly.
abnormal: Calf swelling at least 3 cm greater than the asymptomatic side.
Pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg.
Entire leg swollen.
Chronic foot and toe swelling with skin thickening.
Bilateral dependent pitting oedema.
implications: A calf difference of at least 3 cm, unilateral pitting oedema or whole-leg swelling contributes to the two-level DVT Wells score.
Foot and toe involvement with chronic skin thickening supports lymphoedema.
Bilateral dependent oedema suggests venous, cardiac, renal, hepatic, medication-related or immobility-related causes.
items.importantLimitation: Oedema is not specific to DVT or cellulitis. Previous surgery, chronic asymmetry, lymphoedema and body habitus may limit measurement.

items.title: Two-level DVT Wells assessment
items.summary: Use only when DVT is clinically suspected. Document each criterion and the alternative diagnosis considered; do not record only the total score.
howToTest: Add 1 point for active cancer: treatment ongoing, within 6 months or palliative.
Add 1 point for paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilisation of a lower extremity.
Add 1 point for being bedridden for at least 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks requiring general or regional anaesthesia.
Add 1 point for localised tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system.
Add 1 point if the entire leg is swollen.
Add 1 point if calf swelling is at least 3 cm greater than the asymptomatic side, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity.
Add 1 point for pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg.
Add 1 point for collateral superficial veins that are non-varicose.
Add 1 point for previously documented DVT.
Subtract 2 points if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
Classify 2 points or more as DVT likely and 1 point or less as DVT unlikely.
normal: DVT unlikely: Wells score 1 point or less, followed by the local D-dimer pathway.
abnormal: DVT likely: Wells score 2 points or more, followed by the local proximal leg vein ultrasound pathway.
implications: The score determines the diagnostic pathway; it does not diagnose or exclude DVT.
Use the local arrangements for D-dimer, imaging, interim anticoagulation, renal assessment and follow-up responsibility.
urgentFeatures: New symptoms suggesting pulmonary embolism.
Delay in access to the required DVT diagnostic pathway.
High bleeding risk or contraindication when interim anticoagulation may be considered.
items.importantLimitation: Do not apply the Wells score as a screening tool to every red leg. It is used after clinical suspicion of DVT has been established.

items.title: Neurovascular examination
howToTest: Compare dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses where palpable.
Assess capillary refill, distal temperature and colour.
Assess light-touch sensation and motor function.
Ask about rest pain, claudication, new numbness and weakness.
Use local vascular assessment pathways when compression is being considered.
normal: Warm, well-perfused foot.
Capillary refill not delayed.
Pulses present and comparable with the opposite side or documented baseline.
Sensation and movement preserved.
abnormal: Cold, pale, cyanosed or mottled foot.
Absent or newly reduced pulses.
Delayed capillary refill.
New sensory loss or weakness.
Tissue loss, gangrene or ischaemic ulceration.
implications: New perfusion or neurological abnormality may indicate limb-threatening arterial compromise.
Compression should not be automatically advised where significant arterial disease has not been excluded through the appropriate pathway.
urgentFeatures: Sudden pain with pallor, pulselessness, coldness, paraesthesia or weakness.
Gangrene or ulceration with limb ischaemia.

items.title: Joint and musculoskeletal examination
howToTest: Identify whether maximal pain and swelling are centred on the ankle, knee, first metatarsophalangeal joint or another joint.
Inspect for effusion, deformity and focal joint swelling.
Assess active movement, then carefully assess passive movement.
Assess weight-bearing and gait where safe.
Examine for local trauma, bony tenderness, tendon injury or muscle injury when suggested by the history.
normal: Full or near-full joint movement without marked pain.
No focal effusion or joint-centred tenderness.
No focal bony tenderness or traumatic deformity.
abnormal: Marked pain with passive movement.
Hot swollen joint with substantial restriction.
Focal effusion or severe joint-centred tenderness.
Inability to weight-bear because of joint pain.
Focal bony tenderness, bruising or traumatic deformity.
implications: A hot, severely painful and restricted joint requires assessment for septic arthritis and crystal arthritis.
Diffuse skin inflammation with preserved painless joint movement is more consistent with a superficial process.
Traumatic findings may require an injury-specific pathway.
urgentFeatures: Suspected septic arthritis.
Neurovascular compromise.
Suspected fracture or compartment syndrome.

items.title: Wound, ulcer and diabetic-foot assessment
howToTest: Inspect all wounds and ulcers for size, depth, location, discharge, odour, surrounding erythema and tissue loss.
Assess whether redness, warmth, swelling or pain extends beyond the ulcer margin.
Look for exposed or palpable bone, deep sinus, fluctuance, gangrene or spreading infection.
In diabetes, inspect the entire foot including the plantar surface, heels and between the toes.
Assess perfusion and sensation and determine whether the problem meets the local active diabetic-foot criteria.
Consider a microbiological sample only when indicated by the relevant wound or cellulitis guidance; do not swab intact skin.
normal: No ulcer, wound or portal of entry.
No purulence, deep tissue exposure, gangrene or spreading inflammation.
abnormal: Ulcer with spreading erythema, warmth, swelling or increased pain.
Purulent discharge or fluctuance.
Deep ulcer, exposed bone or suspected osteomyelitis.
Gangrene or associated ischaemia.
Interdigital fissuring or fungal change providing a possible portal of entry.
implications: An ulcer may be colonised without being infected; diagnose infection from clinical signs rather than a positive swab alone.
A limb-threatening diabetic foot problem requires immediate acute referral.
Other active diabetic-foot problems require prompt referral through the local multidisciplinary pathway.

items.title: Venous and lymphatic features
howToTest: Inspect for varicose veins, haemosiderin pigmentation, gaiter-region eczema, induration and venous ulceration.
Assess whether symptoms worsen with dependency and improve with elevation.
Assess chronicity, foot and toe involvement, skin thickening and tissue fibrosis.
Check for previous lymph-node surgery, radiotherapy or known lymphoedema.
Compare with previous photographs, measurements or documented baseline where available.
normal: No chronic venous skin change, varicosities or longstanding oedema.
No foot or toe swelling, skin thickening or fibrosis.
abnormal: Gaiter-region pigmentation, scaling, eczema or induration.
Varicosities and chronic dependent oedema.
Foot and toe involvement with skin thickening or fibrosis.
Chronic asymmetrical swelling with recurrent cellulitis.
implications: Chronic venous disease may mimic or predispose to cellulitis.
Lymphoedema may produce chronic swelling and skin change and increases cellulitis risk.
Acute inflammation can occur on top of chronic venous or lymphatic disease; compare with baseline.

sections.title: Common examination patterns
sections.intro: Patterns support clinical reasoning but do not independently confirm or exclude a diagnosis. More than one process may coexist.

items.title: Cellulitis or erysipelas
commonFindings: Acute or subacute unilateral spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness and swelling.
Possible portal of entry such as a wound, ulcer, fissure, interdigital fungal change or skin trauma.
Skin may be diffusely tender and indurated.
Fever or systemic symptoms may be present but can be absent.
Joint movement is not markedly restricted unless inflammation overlies or involves a joint.
implications: Supports cellulitis when compatible with the history and after important mimics and deeper infection have been considered.
Follow current Northern Ireland antimicrobial guidance for treatment choice, allergy alternatives, dose, renal adjustment and review.

keyTriggers: Suspected abscess, deep infection, osteomyelitis, foreign body or alternative diagnosis requiring imaging.
guidance: Cellulitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis; routine imaging is not required for an uncomplicated presentation.

items.importantLimitation: Bilateral cellulitis is uncommon. Bilateral chronic erythema, itch, scaling, pigmentation and oedema should prompt active consideration of venous or inflammatory skin disease.

items.title: Deep vein thrombosis
commonFindings: Unilateral leg swelling or pain.
Deep venous distribution tenderness.
Entire-leg swelling or calf asymmetry.
Pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg.
Relevant provoking factors or previous DVT.
implications: Use the two-level DVT Wells score and local diagnostic pathway when DVT is clinically suspected.

preferredImaging: Proximal leg vein ultrasound through the local DVT pathway.
keyTriggers: DVT likely: Wells score 2 points or more.
Positive D-dimer after a DVT-unlikely score.
Persistent clinical concern despite an alternative diagnosis.
guidance: Where DVT is likely, NICE recommends ultrasound with the result available within 4 hours if possible, or the interim anticoagulation and imaging-within-24-hours pathway when timely imaging is unavailable.

items.importantLimitation: Clinical examination and inflammatory markers cannot independently exclude DVT. Cellulitis and DVT may coexist.

items.title: Venous eczema or stasis dermatitis
commonFindings: Chronic or recurrent lower-leg erythema, often bilateral.
Itch, dryness, scaling, crusting, weeping or excoriation.
Gaiter-region pigmentation, varicosities and dependent oedema.
Symptoms may worsen later in the day and improve with elevation.
Less focal tenderness and less rapid progression than typical cellulitis.
implications: Supports chronic venous inflammation rather than primary bacterial cellulitis.
Assess for superimposed infection, ulceration and arterial suitability before any compression pathway.

keyTriggers: Concern for DVT, arterial disease, ulcer complication or another diagnosis.
guidance: Use local venous-disease, tissue-viability and compression-assessment pathways.

items.importantLimitation: Venous eczema and cellulitis may coexist, particularly where skin integrity is impaired.

items.title: Lipodermatosclerosis
commonFindings: Chronic venous disease with painful induration in the gaiter region.
Hyperpigmentation, fibrosis and an inverted-champagne-bottle leg shape in established disease.
An acute inflammatory phase may be red, warm and tender.
Usually associated with longstanding oedema or other venous signs.
implications: May mimic cellulitis. Consider venous disease when the pattern is chronic, gaiter-predominant and accompanied by pigmentation or fibrosis.

keyTriggers: Concern for DVT, ulcer complication or significant arterial disease.
guidance: Use local venous and tissue-viability pathways.

items.title: Lymphoedema
commonFindings: Chronic limb heaviness and swelling.
Foot and toe involvement.
Pitting may be present early, with firmer fibrotic tissue and skin thickening later.
Asymmetry may be longstanding.
History of lymph-node surgery, radiotherapy, malignancy or recurrent cellulitis.
implications: Supports lymphatic oedema. Assess carefully for superimposed cellulitis and follow the local lymphoedema pathway.

keyTriggers: New unexplained unilateral swelling, suspected DVT, malignancy or acute infection.
guidance: Do not assume all new redness in a chronically swollen limb is baseline lymphoedema.

items.importantLimitation: A chronically abnormal limb can still develop DVT, cellulitis or acute arterial compromise.

items.title: Superficial thrombophlebitis
commonFindings: Localised linear erythema and tenderness following a superficial vein.
Palpable firm or tender cord.
Usually more focal than cellulitis or DVT.
Possible associated varicose veins, cannulation or local trauma.
implications: Supports superficial venous thrombosis, but assess extent, proximity to the deep venous system and DVT risk through the local pathway.

preferredImaging: Venous ultrasound when required by the local superficial-vein thrombosis pathway.
keyTriggers: Extensive symptoms.
Proximity to the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction.
Concurrent DVT features or significant venous thromboembolism risk.
guidance: Do not assume a superficial palpable cord excludes concurrent DVT.

items.title: Gout or inflammatory arthritis
commonFindings: Redness and swelling centred on a joint.
Marked joint tenderness.
Pain with active and passive movement.
Previous similar self-limiting episodes or established gout.
Possible tophus or involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
implications: Supports crystal or inflammatory arthritis, but septic arthritis must be actively considered in every acutely painful red swollen joint.

keyTriggers: Clinical suspicion of septic arthritis.
Trauma or concern for fracture.
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring aspiration or specialist assessment.
guidance: A normal serum urate during an acute flare does not independently exclude gout.

items.importantLimitation: Do not diagnose gout solely from redness at a typical joint or a previous history of gout.

items.title: Suspected septic arthritis
commonFindings: Acute hot swollen joint.
Severe joint-centred pain.
Marked restriction of active and passive movement.
Inability to weight-bear.
Fever or systemic symptoms may be present but can be absent.
implications: Requires immediate referral through the local septic-joint pathway.

preferredImaging: Joint aspiration and imaging directed by the receiving specialist pathway.
keyTriggers: Clinical suspicion of septic arthritis.
guidance: Do not delay referral while awaiting routine blood tests or plain imaging.

items.importantLimitation: Normal temperature, normal inflammatory markers or a history of gout do not safely exclude septic arthritis.

items.title: Contact dermatitis or inflammatory bite reaction
commonFindings: Itch predominates over pain.
Sharply patterned rash corresponding to an exposure.
Vesicles, weeping or superficial excoriation.
Identifiable punctum or localised bite reaction.
Limited systemic disturbance.
implications: Supports a non-infectious inflammatory cause. Assess for secondary infection when warmth, spreading tenderness, purulence or systemic symptoms develop.

keyTriggers: Retained foreign body, deep collection, significant systemic reaction or diagnostic uncertainty.

items.title: Trauma or haematoma
commonFindings: Clear traumatic onset or local impact.
Bruising, localised swelling and tenderness.
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use may increase the extent of bruising.
Symptoms correspond to the injured tissue rather than a spreading cutaneous pattern.
implications: Supports traumatic soft-tissue injury or haematoma, but assess for fracture, compartment syndrome, ongoing bleeding and infection.

preferredImaging: Imaging directed by the injury-specific clinical decision rule or local pathway.
keyTriggers: Focal bony tenderness, inability to weight-bear, deformity, neurovascular abnormality or escalating tense swelling.

items.importantLimitation: Minor or unremembered trauma does not adequately explain rapidly progressive erythema, severe pain or systemic illness.

items.title: Systemic or dependent bilateral oedema
commonFindings: Bilateral pitting oedema.
Relatively symmetrical distribution.
Limited focal warmth or tenderness.
Associated heart-failure, renal, hepatic, medication or immobility-related features.
Weight change, breathlessness, orthopnoea or reduced urine output may be present depending on the cause.
implications: Consider a systemic or medication-related cause rather than bilateral cellulitis.
Assess for asymmetry, skin breakdown or superimposed infection.

keyTriggers: Clinical features suggesting acute heart failure, renal deterioration, DVT or another acute cause.
guidance: Investigations should be directed by the suspected systemic cause and whether the result will alter management or disposition.

items.title: Diabetic foot infection
commonFindings: Diabetes with an ulcer, wound, fissure or other active foot problem.
Local warmth, erythema, swelling, purulence or increasing pain, noting that neuropathy may reduce pain.
Possible ischaemia, gangrene, deep tissue involvement or exposed bone.
Systemic illness may indicate severe infection.
implications: Use the dedicated diabetic-foot pathway rather than the generic cellulitis pathway.

preferredImaging: Imaging for suspected deep soft-tissue or bone infection through the multidisciplinary diabetic-foot pathway.
keyTriggers: Ulceration with fever or sepsis features.
Ulceration with limb ischaemia.
Deep soft-tissue or bone infection.
Gangrene.
guidance: Limb-threatening or life-threatening diabetic-foot disease requires immediate acute-service referral.
Other active diabetic-foot problems require referral within 1 working day for specialist triage according to local arrangements.

items.importantLimitation: Neuropathy may blunt pain and inflammatory signs. A relatively painless foot lesion may still be limb threatening.

sections.title: Focused safety-netting
sections.intro: Use the standard emergency statement, then add the diagnosis-specific warning features and the planned review interval.

items.title: Red or swollen leg
safetyNetting: Call 999 for significant deterioration in breathing, chest pain or collapse.

Seek urgent reassessment for rapidly spreading redness or swelling; severe or escalating pain; blistering, skin blackening or new numbness; a cold, pale or weak limb; new fever, rigors, confusion or marked general deterioration; inability to stand or walk; or a newly hot, severely painful and restricted joint.
When treated for cellulitis, seek reassessment if symptoms worsen at any time or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days. Skin colour and swelling may take longer to return fully to normal.
Follow the arranged DVT, wound, diabetic-foot, vascular, tissue-viability or hospital-at-home review plan and seek help promptly if the expected contact or investigation does not occur.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting does not make discharge appropriate when serious pathology has not been adequately excluded, the diagnosis remains unsafe or follow-up cannot be delivered.
